The bishop does not say to us, “Receive riches and use them however you want.” Instead, he says to us, “Receive the care of souls, for which you will have to give an account on the day of judgment.” This is something we must fear greatly. This is truly terrifying for us.

There is no calling on earth that could serve God more pleasingly than ours as priests, because we could save both ourselves and others. After all, any one of us loves more the servant who brings ten, or twenty, or even more sheaves into his barn than the servant who brings only one—that is, the one who saves only himself.

Therefore the Lord says to Peter, “If you love me, feed my sheep”—that is, feed them with spiritual pastures.

We ought to be intercessors for human beings before almighty God. We ought to be mediators between God and humanity. But how can we intercede for them, when we ourselves have offended God and lack his grace?
chunks.notes: “Plasphematur” is a spelling error for “blasphematur.” The opening apostolic quotation echoes Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter two, verse twenty-four, though no citation is printed. “Sacerdotes mali ruina sunt populi” is attributed in the text to Gregory. The prophetic language echoes Ezekiel, especially chapter thirty-four and chapter three, but no formal citations are printed. The printed “Sanguinem mei” is likely corrupt; the sense has been translated as “their blood.” The printed “Ne cum aliis predicatio” is corrupt for the Pauline sense, “after preaching to others”; the quotation echoes Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter nine, verse twenty-seven. The printed “Ideo petro a domino” is best understood as “therefore it is said to Peter by the Lord”; the saying echoes the Gospel of John, chapter twenty-one, verse seventeen. The manuscript numerals “.x.” and “.xx.” have been spoken as “ten” and “twenty.”

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Church Building and the Temple of the Heart
chunks.latin: XXII. In dedicatione.
chunks.english: Sermon 22. On the Dedication.
chunks.notes: “In dedicatione” refers to a sermon for the dedication of a church.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quamvis deus presens sit in omni loco ubicumque invocatur nomen eius, tamen specialiter elegit sibi domum ubi ab omnibus conveniatur et sacrificium ei offeratur, et ubi angelos suos custodes die et nocte deputavit, qui offerant orationes nostras coram ipso, et ubi ab omnibus invocaretur, et ubi fides catholica predicaretur, ut esset omnibus una fides, unum baptisma, et ut omnes unum in christo sentirent. Ideo, fratres karissimi, qui hodie convenistis in honore domini nostri ihesu christi et sancte dedicationis, preparate deo quoque aliud templum, cuius figura est illud lapideum. Preparate deo dignam domum in corde vestro, et mundate illud ab omni odio, fornicatione, adulterio, periurio, avaricia, Gula, ebrietate. Cuiuscumque cor ab his et similibus possessum est, ab illo fugit deus. Et postquam has sordes expurgetis, ornate templum illud: Humilitate, castitate, continentia, vigiliis, ieiuniis, elemosinis, orationibus et ceteris bonis operibus; et accendite ibi lumen sancte confessionis et vere penitentie, et perfundite lacrimis illud, et accendite ibi odorem sancte caritatis in deum et proximum vestrum. Tunc habitabit in corde vestro, et mansionem apud vos faciet, et eritis deo verum templum, de quo dicit apostolus: Templum dei sanctum est, quod estis vos. Hoc modo, sicut prediximus, promeruit publicanus hacheus, de quo hodie lectum est in evangelio, quod deus dignatus est in domo illius manere, et indulsit ei omnia peccata sua, quia ei locum vere penitentie preparavit. Unde vos, fratres karissimi, invitate deum in domum cordis vestri, et offerte ei sacrificium bone voluntatis, ut ipse vos post hanc vitam recipiat in eterna tabernacula. Quod ipse p.
chunks.english:
Although God is present in every place where his name is invoked, he has nevertheless chosen a house for himself in a special way: a place where everyone may gather, where sacrifice may be offered to him, and where he has appointed his guardian angels day and night to present our prayers before him. It is a place where all may call upon him, and where the catholic faith may be preached, so that there may be for all one faith, one baptism, and so that all may be of one mind in Christ.

Therefore, dearest brothers, you who have gathered today in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of this holy dedication: prepare another temple for God, of which this stone building is the figure. Prepare a worthy house for God in your heart. Cleanse it from all hatred, fornication, adultery, perjury, greed, gluttony, and drunkenness. From the person whose heart is possessed by these and similar sins, God flees.

And after you have cleared out this filth, adorn that temple with humility, chastity, self-control, vigils, fasting, almsgiving, prayers, and the other good works. Light there the lamp of holy confession and true repentance. Bathe it with tears. Kindle there the fragrance of holy charity toward God and toward your neighbor.

Then God will dwell in your heart and make his home with you. You will be a true temple for God. As the apostle says, “The temple of God is holy, and that temple is you.”

In this way, as we said before, Zacchaeus the tax collector—about whom today’s Gospel reading spoke—earned the grace that God deigned to remain in his house and forgave him all his sins, because Zacchaeus prepared for him a place of true repentance.

So then, dearest brothers, invite God into the house of your heart, and offer him the sacrifice of a good will, so that after this life he may receive you into the eternal dwellings. May he himself grant this.
chunks.notes: The phrase “one faith, one baptism” echoes Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter four, verse five, though no reference is printed. The temple quotation echoes Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, verse seventeen, though no reference is printed. The printed name “hacheus” is a corrupt form of “Zacchaeus,” translated accordingly; the Gospel episode is in the Gospel of Luke, chapter nineteen. The final abbreviation “Quod ipse p.” is expanded in sense as the usual closing formula, “May he himself grant this.”

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Chapter 23: On the Day of a Funeral
chunks.latin: XXIII. In die exequiarum.
chunks.english: Sermon 23. On the day of a funeral.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Scriptum est in libris quia melior est dies mortis dies nativitatis, et melius ire ad domum luctus quam ad domum convivii. Qui hoc prescripsit nobis, ille scivit bene miseriam et laborem huius vite. Statim ut nascimur incipimus plorare; hec prima vox nostra est, et ita quamdiu vivimus semper in labore et miseriis sumus. Ecce videtis reges et duces, comites et alios divites, quomodo laborant, in quibus angustiis nocte et die versantur. Divites eodem modo ut pauperes captivantur, occiduntur, multa adversa paciuntur, et usque ad diem mortis numquam erunt in pace; et in die mortis sue solvuntur a malis omnibus huius seculi, et tunc incipit eterna requies et eterna leticia [f. 14v] omnibus illis qui in hoc mundo deum timuerint et eius voluntatem impleverint. Tunc cessat omnis miseria, tunc cessat fnales et sitis, tunc cessat omnis lapor. Ubi nulla pestis, nullus hostis, ibi chorus angelorum, ibi videbimus filium dei ad dexteram patris, ibi regnabimus cum christo in perpetuum.
chunks.english:
It is written in the sacred books that the day of death is better than the day of birth, and that it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting. The one who wrote this for our instruction knew well the misery and toil of this life.

As soon as we are born, we begin to cry. That is our first voice. And so, as long as we live, we are always amid labor and troubles. Look at kings and rulers, counts and other wealthy people. See how they struggle, and what anxieties they endure night and day. The rich, just like the poor, are taken captive, killed, and made to suffer many hardships. Until the day of their death they are never truly at peace.

But on the day of their death they are released from all the evils of this world. Then eternal rest and eternal joy begin for all who have feared God in this world and done his will. Then every misery ends. Then hunger and thirst end. Then every labor ends. There, where there is no plague and no enemy, there is the choir of angels. There we shall see the Son of God at the right hand of the Father. There we shall reign with Christ forever.
chunks.notes: The opening sentence echoes Ecclesiastes, but the Latin gives no formal citation. The printed reading “fnales” appears to be corrupt; I translated the evident sense as “hunger,” reading “fames.” The printed “lapor” appears to be a misspelling of “labor.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Fratres karissimi, debetis quoque scire quare melius sit vobis ire ad domum ubi mortuos videmus et ubi gemitus et planctus est, quam ad convivia ubi leticia est: quia ubi mortuos videmus, statim quoque cogitamus quid futurum sit de nobis, et ubi cogitamus quoque ad quem finem veniat et vita et substantia nostra et omnis secularis gloria. Et commonemur quoque quia omnia nostra debemus hic relinquere, et quia nudi intravimus, nudi exibimus; tunc primum ignorabimus cui congregavimus, et quomodo statim incipimus putrescere, et tunc alii incipiunt uti bonis nostris, et nihil umquam remanet nobis de omnibus bonis nostris nisi forte aliquid premisissemus. Bona opera nostra et bona voluntas nostra tantum nobiscum remanet.
chunks.english:
Dearest brothers, you should also know why it is better for you to go to the house where we see the dead, where there is groaning and mourning, than to go to feasts where there is gladness. When we see the dead, we immediately think about what will happen to us. We think about the end to which our life, our possessions, and all worldly glory are coming.

We are reminded that we must leave everything we have here, and that as we entered naked, so we shall leave naked. Only then will we realize that we do not know for whom we gathered all these things. Soon we begin to decay, and others begin to use our goods. Nothing from all our possessions ever remains with us, unless perhaps we sent something ahead beforehand. Only our good works and our good will remain with us.
chunks.notes: “Sent something ahead” means almsgiving and good works performed before death.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Et pro certo scire debetis quia in transitu uniuscuiusque nostrum aderunt angeli dei et angeli diaboli, et utrique suam partem exigunt. Si maiora sunt opera bona, angeli dei prevalebunt et rapiunt animam in paradysum in conspectu dei. Si autem plura sunt opera mala, tunc prevalebunt nuncii diaboli et ducunt animam in conspectum diaboli, ut in [f. 15r] eterno igne sine fine ardeat. Ideo rogo vos propter omnipotentem deum ut adtendatis periculum vestrum quod vobis futurum sit, et rememoramini diem novissimum vestrum, et preparate vos ad illum locum ubi vos ipse christus cum angelis suis expectat et quo vos invitat. Orate hodie omnipotentem deum ut causa sancte marie matris sue et omnium angelorum suorum animam cuius boni hominis eripiat de potestate diaboli, et conservet eam ad eternam requiem et ad eternam leticiam, que numquam deficiet.
chunks.english:
And you should know this for certain: at the passing of each one of us, the angels of God and the angels of the devil will be present, and both sides will claim what belongs to them. If the good works are greater, the angels of God will prevail and carry the soul away into paradise, before the face of God. But if the evil works are more numerous, then the messengers of the devil will prevail and lead the soul before the devil, so that it may burn without end in eternal fire.

Therefore I beg you, for the sake of almighty God, pay attention to the danger that lies ahead of you. Remember your last day. Prepare yourselves for that place where Christ himself, with his angels, is waiting for you and inviting you.

Today pray to almighty God that, through the intercession of holy Mary his mother and of all his angels, he may rescue the soul of this good man from the power of the devil, and preserve it for eternal rest and eternal joy, which will never fail.
chunks.notes: The phrase “causa sancte marie matris sue” is idiomatic and has been rendered as “through the intercession of holy Mary his mother.” The phrase “cuius boni hominis” is grammatically awkward in the manuscript; I translated the evident funeral context as “of this good man.”

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Chapter 24: Honoring the Lord’s Day
chunks.latin: XXIV. Dominica die.
chunks.english: Sermon 24. On Sunday.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Omnem dominicum diem honorare debemus cum omni studio honoris et sanctitatis, quia dominicus dies est primus dies in quo christus mundum cepit operari. In ipso creati sunt angeli. In ipso primum manna israhelitico populo veniebat. In ipso christus resurrexit a mortuis. In ipso spiritus sanctus apostolis datus est; et ipse ultimus dies est huius seculi, in quo et nos resurrecturi sumus, et in quo unusquisque premium secundum opera sua recepturus est. Ideo placuit apostolis ut dominicus dies sine omni servili opere servaretur, et inde dominicus dies appellatus est, quod nichil liceat nobis in illa die operari quod displiceat domino nostro. Quapropter quia hodie in illis operibus que deo placent studere debemus, Ideo congruum videbatur referre [f. 15v] vobis de dignitate et sanctitate huius diei, ut his auditis terrore et amore deum amplectamini, et sic vestre anime consolamini, et in eo bonis bonis operibus insidare debemus.
chunks.english:
We must honor every Lord’s Day with every effort toward reverence and holiness, because the Lord’s Day is the first day, the day on which Christ began to make the world. On that day the angels were created. On that day manna first came to the people of Israel. On that day Christ rose from the dead. On that day the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles. And that same day will be the last day of this world, the day on which we too will rise again, and on which each person will receive a reward according to his works.

For this reason it pleased the apostles that the Lord’s Day should be kept free from every servile work. And it is called the Lord’s Day because on that day we are not allowed to do anything that displeases our Lord.

Therefore, since today we must devote ourselves to the works that please God, it seemed fitting to speak to you about the dignity and holiness of this day. When you have heard this, may you embrace God with both fear and love, may you thus comfort your souls; and on this day we ought to devote ourselves to good works.
chunks.notes: The last clause is corrupt or at least badly transmitted: “bonis bonis operibus insidare debemus.” I translated the probable sense as “devote yourselves to good works,” perhaps reading “bonis operibus insudare” or a similar expression.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Chapter 25: Prayer and the Rogation Days
chunks.latin: XXV. Quando volueris.
chunks.english: Sermon 25. Whenever you wish.
chunks.notes: The Latin heading “Quando volueris” literally means “When you wish,” probably indicating that this sermon may be used on an appropriate occasion.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Diligenter, filii et fratres karissimi, in corporis et cordis aure verba dei percipite, piis moribusque adimplete. Sciens enim dominus post liberi arbitrii amissionem nullum bonum a nobis posse esse, non solum ad orandum devote sed et instanter hortatur, et monet ut quod nature possibilitas minus habet ab illo sine quo boni quid agi non potest orando inveniat. Adeamus ergo eum iuxta evangelii parabolam nocte tribulationis, eiusque auxilium, qui suos in mundo pressuram habituros esse predixit, suppliciter flagitemus, ut sicut ipse mundum vicit, sic nos vincere faciat.
chunks.english:
Listen carefully, dearest children and brothers. Receive the words of God with the ear of the body and with the ear of the heart, and fulfill them by living in holy ways.

The Lord knows that, after the loss of free will, no good can come from us by ourselves. Therefore he urges us not only to pray devoutly, but to pray persistently. He teaches us that whatever human nature lacks in its own power, it should seek through prayer from him, without whom nothing good can be done.

So let us come to him, as in the Gospel parable, in the night of tribulation. Let us humbly beg for the help of the one who foretold that his own people would suffer hardship in this world, so that, just as he conquered the world, he may make us conquer too.
chunks.notes: The “Gospel parable” refers to the friend asking for bread at midnight, but no formal biblical citation is printed in the Latin.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Et quia omnipotens interdum peticionem differt, non ut premium minuat sed ut meritum augeat, instanter petamus ut tres panes nobis tribuat. Per panem quippe, qui principalis est victus, noticiam sancte trinitatis vel tres principales virtutes, fidem, spem, caritatem, quibus ad celestia gradiamur, designat. Hoc instanter petamus, et si non propter amiciciam, saltem propter inprobitatem surgens necessaria dabit. Vult enim deus inportunos habere petitores, et sua gratuita dona nostra ultra [f. 16r] esse merita. Semper enim aures divine pietatis nostris orationibus sunt aperte, si a precibus non cessemus et in fide non dubitemus. Si enim carnalis pater bona data dare filiis novit, quanto magis pater celestis dabit spiritum suum petetentibus?
chunks.english:
And because the Almighty sometimes delays what we ask—not in order to lessen the reward, but to increase our merit—let us ask persistently that he give us the three loaves.

Bread is our most basic food. Here it signifies either the knowledge of the Holy Trinity, or the three principal virtues: faith, hope, and love, by which we make our way toward heaven. Let us ask for this persistently. And if the friend will not rise because of friendship, then at least because of our insistence he will rise and give what is needed.

God wants his petitioners to be persistent. His gifts are free, and they go beyond what we deserve. The ears of divine mercy are always open to our prayers, if we do not stop praying and do not waver in faith. For if an earthly father knows how to give good gifts to his children, how much more will the heavenly Father give his Spirit to those who ask him?
chunks.notes: The discussion continues the Gospel parable of the three loaves and also echoes Gospel teaching on the Father giving good gifts, but the Latin provides no printed citation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Confiteamur ergo alterutrum peccata nostra, et pro invicem ut salvemur oremus. Multum enim assidua deprecatio valet. Celum namque oratio clausit et aperuit. Sed quia rogationum dies annuatim recolimus, commemorare libet unde exordium sumpsit. Peccatis exigentibus, luporum rabie acriter inminente, galliarum episcopi apud viennam congregati in commune hos dies triduo celebrari statuerunt. Cumque dominus pestem misericorditer abstulisset, hi dies in consuetudinem annue celebritatis venerunt, ut per galliarum provincias ante ascensionem domini celebrarentur.
chunks.english:
So let us confess our sins to one another, and pray for one another so that we may be saved. Constant prayer is very powerful. Prayer closed heaven, and prayer opened it again.

Since we celebrate the Rogation Days every year, I would like to recall where they began. Because of the people’s sins, a fierce plague of wolves was threatening them. The bishops of Gaul gathered at Vienne, and together they decreed that these days should be celebrated for three days. And when the Lord mercifully removed the plague, these days became an annual custom, to be celebrated throughout the provinces of Gaul before the Lord’s Ascension.
chunks.notes: The statements about confessing sins to one another and the power of prayer echo the Letter of James and the story of Elijah, but no formal citations are printed in the Latin. “Viennam” refers to Vienne in Gaul.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Agamus et nos hos dies, sicut statutum est in conciliis, cum summa reverentia et devotione, cum abstinentia carnis et humilitate cordis, ut non visibilium luporum rabiem evadamus, sed ut invisibilium, videlicet spirituum inmundorum, temptamenta vincere valeamus. Nullus his diebus preciosis vestimentis induatur, sed in sacco et cinere lugere a patribus statutum est. Prohibeantur ebrietates et commessationes. Nemo ibi equitare presumat, et discalciatis [f. 16v] pedibus omnes incedamus, et cum contritione cordis dei misericordiam exoremus pro peccatis, et non solum pro nostris sed pro tocius ecclesie necessitatibus; supplicemus pro omnibus hominibus, pro domino apostolico, pro rege et his qui in sublimitate sunt constituti, pro clero et omni populo catholico, ut in omni sanctitate quietam et tranquillam vitam agamus. Hoc enim acceptum est coram deo, qui vult omnes homines salvos fieri et ad agnitionem venire. Qui uu[…]
chunks.english:
Let us also keep these days, as has been decreed in the councils, with the greatest reverence and devotion: with abstinence from meat and with humility of heart. We do this not merely to escape the fury of visible wolves, but so that we may overcome the temptations of invisible wolves—that is, unclean spirits.

On these days no one should dress in costly clothing. Our fathers decreed that we should mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Drunkenness and feasting must be forbidden. No one should presume to ride on horseback there. Let us all walk barefoot, and with contrition of heart let us implore God’s mercy for our sins—not only for our own sins, but for the needs of the whole Church.

Let us pray for all people: for the lord pope, for the king and those placed in high office, for the clergy, and for the whole Catholic people, so that we may live a quiet and peaceful life in all holiness. This is pleasing before God, who wants all people to be saved and to come to knowledge. He who...
chunks.notes: The final words “Qui uu[…]” are truncated in the supplied text. I have left the English deliberately incomplete as “He who...” rather than inventing a conclusion. The line about praying for all people and rulers, and about God wanting all to be saved, echoes Paul’s first letter to Timothy, but the Latin gives no citation.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Chapter 26: Dedicating the Church and the Heart
chunks.latin: XXVI. In dedicatione.
chunks.english: Sermon 26. On the Dedication.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Fratres karissimi, qui hodie convenistis in honore domini nostri ihesu et sancte dedicationis, preparate deo et ornate illud templum cuius figura est istud lapideum. Quia quamvis deus presens sit in omni loco ubicumque invocatur nomen eius, tamen specialiter elegit sibi domum ubi ab omnibus conveniatur, et sacrificium ei offeratur, et ubi angelos suos custodes die et nocte deputavit, qui offerant orationes nostras coram ipso, et ubi ab omnibus invocaretur, et ubi fides catholica predicaretur, ut esset omnibus una fides, unum baptisma, et ut unum in christo sentirent. Ideo vos preparate deo dignam domum in corde vestro, et mundate illud ab omni odio, fornicatione, adulterio, periurio, avaricia, gula, ebrietate et cetera. Cuiuscumque cor ab his et similibus possessum est, ab illo fugit deus. Et quidam
chunks.english:
Dearest brothers, you have gathered today in honor of our Lord Jesus and of this holy dedication. So prepare for God, and adorn for him, that temple of which this stone church is only a figure.

Although God is present in every place where his name is invoked, he has nevertheless chosen a house for himself in a special way: a place where all may gather, where sacrifice may be offered to him, where he has appointed his guardian angels day and night to present our prayers before him, where he may be invoked by all, and where the Catholic faith may be preached. In this way there may be one faith for all, one baptism, and all may be of one mind in Christ.

Therefore prepare a worthy house for God in your heart. Cleanse it from all hatred, sexual immorality, adultery, perjury, greed, gluttony, drunkenness, and the like. God flees from anyone whose heart is possessed by these and similar sins. And some...
chunks.notes: The supplied text breaks off after “Et quidam,” meaning “And some...” I have not supplied a continuation.
